entries.316f26a787178f32ed8a5483555903d428956e8f: <div sID="gen20779" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Zech.2" sID="Zech.2"/> <div eID="gen20779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20780" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20781" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. Another vision which the prophet saw, not for his own entertainment, but for his satisfaction and the edification of those to whom he was sent, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.1-Zech.2.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. A sermon upon it, in the rest of the chapter, 1. By way of explication of the vision, showing it to be a prediction of the replenishing of Jerusalem and of its safety and honour, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.3-Zech.2.5">ver. 3-5</reference>. 2. By way of application. Here is, (1.) A use of exhortation to the Jews that were yet in Babylon, pressing them to hasten their return to their own land, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.6-Zech.2.9">ver. 6-9</reference>. (2.) A use of consolation to those that were returned, in reference to the many difficulties they had to struggle with, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.10-Zech.2.12">ver. 10-12</reference>. (3.) A use of caution to all not to prescribe to God, or limit him, but patiently to wait for him, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.13">ver. 13</reference>.
entries.b1d8aca2c279b3d96c441ffffc0a8ff3917cb8f4: <div eID="gen20781" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20780" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Measuring Line. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 520.)</title> <div sID="gen20782" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I lifted up mine eyes again, and looked, and behold a man with a measuring line in his hand. <hi type="super">2</hi> Then said I, Whither goest thou? And he said unto me, To measure Jerusalem, to see what <hi type="italic">is</hi> the breadth thereof, and what <hi type="italic">is</hi> the length thereof. <hi type="super">3</hi> And, behold, the angel that talked with me went forth, and another angel went out to meet him, <hi type="super">4</hi> And said unto him, Run, speak to this young man, saying, Jerusalem shall be inhabited <hi type="italic">as</hi> towns without walls for the multitude of men and cattle therein: <hi type="super">5</hi> For I, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , will be unto her a wall of fire round about, and will be the glory in the midst of her. <div eID="gen20782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20783" type="x-p"/> This prophet was ordered, in God's name, to assure the people (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.16">ch. i. 16</reference>) that a <hi type="italic">line should be stretched forth upon Jerusalem.</hi> Now here we have that promise illustrated and confirmed, that the prophet might deliver that part of his message to the people with the more clearness and assurance. <div eID="gen20783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20784" type="x-p"/> I. He sees, in a vision, a man going to measure Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.1-Zech.2.2">v. 1, 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">He lifted up his eyes again, and looked.</hi> God had shown him that which was very encouraging to him, (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.20">ch. i. 20</reference>), and therefore now he <hi type="italic">lifted up his eyes again and looked.</hi> Note, The comfortable sights which by faith we have had of God's goodness made to pass before us should engage us to lift up our eyes again, and to search further into the discoveries made to us of the divine grace; for there is still more to be seen. In the close of the foregoing chapter he had seen Jerusalem's enemies baffled and broken, so that now he begins to hope she shall not be ruined. But that is not enough to make her happy, and therefore that is not all that is promised. Here is more carpenter's work to be done. When David had resolved to <hi type="italic">cut off the horns of the wicked</hi> he engaged likewise that the <hi type="italic">horns of the righteous</hi> should be <hi type="italic">exalted,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.75.10">Ps. lxxv. 10</reference>. And so does the <hi type="italic">Son of David</hi> here; for he is <hi type="italic">the man,</hi> even <hi type="italic">the man Christ Jesus,</hi> whom the prophet sees <hi type="italic">with a measuring line in his hand;</hi> for he is the master builder of his church (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.3">Heb. iii. 3</reference>), and he builds exactly by line and level. Zechariah took the boldness to ask him <hi type="italic">whither he was going</hi> and what he designed to do with that measuring line. And he readily told him that he was going to <hi type="italic">measure Jerusalem,</hi> to take a particular account of the dimensions of it each way, that it might be computed what was necessary for the making of a wall about it, and that it might appear, by comparing its dimensions with the vast numbers that should inhabit it, what additions were necessary to be made for the receiving and containing of them; when multitudes flock to Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.4">Isa. lx. 4</reference>) it is time for her to <hi type="italic">enlarge the place of her tent,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.54.2">Isa. liv. 2</reference>. Note, God takes notice of the extent of his church, and will take care that, when ever so many guests are brought in to the wedding supper, still there <hi type="italic">shall be room,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.14.22">Luke xiv. 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">In</hi> the New Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">my Father's house</hi> above, <hi type="italic">there are many mansions.</hi> <div eID="gen20784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20785" type="x-p"/> II. He is informed that this vision means well to Jerusalem, that the measuring line he saw was not a <hi type="italic">line of confusion</hi> (as that <reference osisRef="Isa.34.11">Isa. xxxiv. 11</reference>), not a line to mete out for destruction, as when God <hi type="italic">purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion he stretched out a line</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.8">Lam. ii. 8</reference>); but it is as when he <hi type="italic">divided the inheritance by line,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.78.55">Ps. lxxviii. 55</reference>. The <hi type="italic">angel that talked with</hi> the prophet <hi type="italic">went forth,</hi> as he designed, <hi type="italic">to measure Jerusalem,</hi> but <hi type="italic">another angel went out to meet him,</hi> to desire that he would first explain this vision to the prophet, that it might not occasion him any uneasy speculations: <hi type="italic">Run, and speak to this young man</hi> (for, it seems, the prophet entered upon his prophecy when he was young, yet no man ought to despise his youth when God thus highly honoured it); he is a young man, not experienced, and may be ready to fear the worst; therefore bid him hope the best; tell him that Jerusalem shall be both safe and great, 1. As safe and great as numbers of men can make it (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Jerusalem shall be inhabited as towns without walls;</hi> the inhabitants of it shall increase, and multiply, and replenish it to admiration, so that it shall extend itself far beyond the present dimensions which now there is an account taken of. The walls of a city, as they defend it, so they straiten and confine it, and keep its inhabitants from multiplying beyond such a pitch; but Jerusalem, even when it is walled, to keep off the enemy, shall be inhabited <hi type="italic">as towns without walls.</hi> The city shall be in a manner lost in the suburbs, as London is, where the out-parishes are more populous than those within the walls. So shall it be with Jerusalem; it shall be extended as freely as if it had no walls at all, and yet shall be as safe as if it had the strongest walls, such a <hi type="italic">multitude of men</hi> (which are the best walls of a city) <hi type="italic">shall there be therein,</hi> and of <hi type="italic">cattle too,</hi> to be not only food, but wealth too, for those men. Note, The increase of the numbers of a people is a great blessing, is a fruit of God's blessing on them and an earnest of further blessings, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.38">Ps. cvii. 38</reference>. <hi type="italic">They are multiplied, for he blesses them.</hi> 2. As safe and great as the presence of God can make it, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.5">v. 5</reference>. (1.) It shall be safe, for God himself will be a <hi type="italic">wall of fire round about it.</hi> Jerusalem had no walls about it at this time, but lay naked and exposed; formerly, when it had walls, the enemies not only broke through them, but broke them down; but now God will be unto her a wall of fire. Some think it alludes to shepherds that made fires about their flocks, or travellers that made fires about their tents in desert places, to frighten wild beasts from them. God will not only <hi type="italic">make a hedge</hi> about them as he did about Job (<reference osisRef="Job.1.10">ch. i. 10</reference>), not only make walls and bulwarks about them, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.1">Isa. xxvi. 1</reference> (those may be battered down), not only be as the mountains round about them, <reference osisRef="Ps.125.2">Ps. cxxv. 2</reference> (mountains may be got over), but he will be a wall of fire round them, which cannot be broken through, nor scaled, nor undermined, nor the foundations of it sapped, nor can it be attempted, or approached, without danger to the assailants. God will not only make a wall of fire about her, but he will himself be such a wall; for <hi type="italic">our God is a consuming fire</hi> to his and his church's enemies. He is a wall of fire, not on one side only, but round about on every side. (2.) It shall be great, for God himself <hi type="italic">will be the glory in the midst of it.</hi> His temple, his altar, shall be set up and attended there, and his institutions observed, and there then shall the tokens of his special presence and favour be, which will be the glory in the midst of them, will make them truly admirable in the eyes of all about them. God will have honour from them, and put honour upon them. Note, Those that have God for their God have him for their glory; those that have him in the midst of them have glory in the midst of them, and thence the church is said to be <hi type="italic">all glorious within.</hi> And those persons and places that have God to be the glory in the midst of them have him for a wall of fire round about them, for <hi type="italic">upon all that glory there is,</hi> and shall be, <hi type="italic">a defence,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Isa. iv. 5</reference>. Now all this was fulfilled in part in Jerusalem, which in process of time became a very flourishing city, and made a very great figure in those parts of the world, much beyond what could have been expected, considering how low it was brought and how long it was ere it recovered itself; but it was to have its full accomplishment in the gospel-church, which is extended far, as towns without walls, by the admission of the Gentiles into it, and which has God, the Son of God, for its prince and protector.
entries.41cb8a714792b1986bd12dea065460306a242989: <div eID="gen20785" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Zion Invited to Liberty. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 520.)</title> <div sID="gen20786" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Ho, ho, <hi type="italic">come forth,</hi> and flee from the land of the north, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : for I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the heaven, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">7</hi> Deliver thyself, O Zion, that dwellest <hi type="italic">with</hi> the daughter of Babylon. <hi type="super">8</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; After the glory hath he sent me unto the nations which spoiled you: for he that toucheth you toucheth the apple of his eye. <hi type="super">9</hi> For, behold, I will shake mine hand upon them, and they shall be a spoil to their servants: and ye shall know that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts hath sent me. <div eID="gen20786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20787" type="x-p"/> One would have thought that Cyrus's proclamation, which gave liberty to the captive Jews to return to their own land, would suffice to bring them all back, and that, as when Pharaoh gave them leave to quit Egypt and their house of bondage there, they would not leave a hoof behind; but it seems it had not that effect. There were about 40,000 whose spirits God stirred up to go, and they went; but many, perhaps the greater part, stayed behind. The land of their captivity was to most of them the land of their nativity; they had taken root there, had gained a settlement, and many of them a very comfortable one; some perhaps had got estates and preferments there, and they did not think they could better themselves by returning to their own land. <hi type="italic">Patria est ubicunque bene est—My country is every spot where I feel myself happy.</hi> They had no great affection to their own land, and apprehended the difficulties in their way to it insuperable. This proceeded from a bad cause—a distrust of the power and promise of God, a love of ease and worldly wealth, and an indifference to the religion of their country and to the God of Israel himself; and it had a bad effect, for it was a tacit censure of those as foolish, rash, and given to change, that did return, and a weakening of their hands in the work of God. Such as these could not sing (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.1-Ps.137.9">Ps. cxxxvii.</reference>) in their captivity, for they had <hi type="italic">forgotten thee, O Jerusalem!</hi> and were so far from preferring thee before their chief joy that they preferred any joy before thee. Here is therefore another proclamation issued out by the God of Israel, strictly charging and commanding all his free-born subjects, wherever they were dispersed, speedily to return into their own land and render themselves at their respective posts there. They are loudly summoned (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Ho! ho! come forth, and flee from the land of the north, saith the Lord.</hi> This fitly follows upon the promise of the rebuilding and enlarging of Jerusalem. If God will build it for them and their comfort, they must come and inhabit it for him and his glory, and not continue sneaking in Babylon. Note, The promises and privileges with which God's people are blessed should engage us, whatever it cost us, to join ourselves to them and <hi type="italic">cast in our lot among them.</hi> When Zion is enlarged, to make room for all God's Israel, it is the greatest madness imaginable for any of them to stay in Babylon. The captivity of a sinful state is by no means to be continued in, though a man be ever so easy upon temporal accounts. No: <hi type="italic">Come forth and flee</hi> with all speed, and lose no time. <hi type="italic">Escape for thy life; look not behind thee.</hi> To induce them to hasten their return, let them consider, 1. They are now dispersed, and are concerned to incorporate themselves for their mutual common defence (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have spread you abroad as the four winds of heaven,</hi> sent some into one corner of the world and some into another; this has been your condition a long time, and therefore you should now think of coming together again, to help one another." God owns that his scattering them was in wrath, and therefore they must take this invitation as a token of God's being willing to be reconciled to them again, so that they kicked at his kindness in refusing to accept the call. 2. They are now in bondage, and are concerned to assert their own liberty; and therefore, "<hi type="italic">Deliver thyself, O Zion!</hi> flee from the oppressor, and make the best of thy way. Let us see some such bold efforts and struggles to help thyself as become the generous gracious seed of Abraham." <reference osisRef="Zech.2.7">v. 7</reference>. Note, When Christ has proclaimed that deliverance to the captives which he has himself wrought out it then concerns each of us to <hi type="italic">deliver ourselves,</hi> to <hi type="italic">loose ourselves from the bands of our necks</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.2">Isa. lii. 2</reference>), and, since we are under grace, to resolve that <hi type="italic">sin shall not have dominion over us,</hi> Zion herself is here said to <hi type="italic">dwell with the daughter of Babylon,</hi> because many of the <hi type="italic">precious sons of Zion</hi> dwelt there, and where the people of God are there the church of God is, for it is not tied to places. Now it is not fit that Zion should dwell with the daughter of Babylon; what communion can light have with darkness? Zion will be in danger of partaking with the daughter of Babylon both <hi type="italic">in her sins</hi> and <hi type="italic">in her plagues;</hi> and therefore, "<hi type="italic">Come out of her, my people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.18.4">Rev. xviii. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">Deliver thyself, O Zion!</hi> by a speedy return to thy own land, and do not destroy thyself by continuing in that polluted devoted land." Those that would be found among the generation of God's children must <hi type="italic">save themselves from</hi> the <hi type="italic">untoward generation</hi> of this world; it was St. Peter's charge to his new converts, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.40">Acts ii. 40</reference>. 3. They have seemed to be forsaken and forgotten of God, but God will now make it to appear that he espouses their cause and will plead it with jealousy, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.8-Zech.2.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. It was a discouragement to those who remained in Babylon to hear of the difficulties and oppositions which their brethren met with that had returned, by which they were still in danger of being crushed and overpowered. "And we might as well sit still" (think they) "as rise up and fall." In answer to this objection, the <hi type="italic">angel that talked with</hi> the prophet (that is, Jesus Christ) tells him what he had commission to do for their protection and the perfecting of their salvation, and herein he has an eye to the great redemption which, in the fulness of time, he was to be the author of. Christ, who is Jehovah, and the <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts,</hi> of all the hosts of heaven and earth, in both which he has a sovereign power, <hi type="italic">says, He</hi> (that is, the Father) <hi type="italic">has sent me.</hi> Note, What Jesus has done, and does, for his church against his enemies, he was sent and commissioned by the Father to do. With great satisfaction he often speaks of <hi type="italic">the Father that sent him.</hi> (1.) He is sent <hi type="italic">after the glory.</hi> After the glorious beginning of their deliverance he is sent to perfect it, for he is the finisher of that work which he is the author of. Christ is sent, in the first place, to the nation and people of the Jews, <hi type="italic">to whom pertained the glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Rom. ix. 4</reference>. And he was himself the <hi type="italic">glory of his people Israel.</hi> But <hi type="italic">after the glory,</hi> after his care of them, he is <hi type="italic">sent to the nations, to be a light to lighten the Gentiles,</hi> by the power of his gospel to captivate them, and bring them, and every high thought among them, into obedience to himself. (2.) He is <hi type="italic">sent to the nations that spoiled them,</hi> to take vengeance on them for the wrongs done to Zion, when the year of his redeemed comes and the <hi type="italic">year of recompences for the controversy of Zion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.34.8">Isa. xxxiv. 8</reference>. He is sent to <hi type="italic">shake his hand upon them,</hi> to lift up his mighty hand against them and to lay upon them his heavy hand, to <hi type="italic">bruise them with a rod of iron</hi> and <hi type="italic">dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.9">Ps. ii. 9</reference>. Some think it intimates how easily God can subdue and humble them with the turn of his hand; it is but shaking his hand over them and the work is done. <hi type="italic">They shall be a spoil to their servants,</hi> shall be enslaved to those whom they had enslaved, and be plundered by those whom they had plundered. In Esther's time this was fulfilled, when the <hi type="italic">Jews had rule over those that hated them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.1">Esth. ix. 1</reference>), and often in the time of the Maccabees. The promise is further fulfilled in Christ's victory over our spiritual enemies, his <hi type="italic">spoiling principalities and powers and making a show of them openly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.2.15">Col. ii. 15</reference>. And it is still in force to the gospel-church. Christ will reckon with all that are enemies to it, and sooner or later will make them <hi type="italic">his footstool,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Ps. cx. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.9">Rev. iii. 9</reference>. (3.) What he will do for his church shall be an evident proof of God's tender care of it and affection to it: <hi type="italic">He that touches you touches the apple of his eye.</hi> This is a high expression of God's love to his church. By his resentment of the injuries done to her it appears how dear she is to him, how he interests himself in all her interests, and takes what is done against her, not only as done against himself, but as done against the very apple of his eye, the tenderest part, which nature has made very fine, has put a double guard upon, and taught us to be in a special manner careful of, and which the least touch is a great offence to. This encourages the people of God to pray with David (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.8">Ps. xvii. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">Keep me as the apple of thy eye;</hi> and engages them to do as Solomon directs (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.2">Prov. vii. 2</reference>), to <hi type="italic">keep his law as the apple of their eye.</hi> Some understand it thus: "<hi type="italic">He that touches you touches the apple of his own eye;</hi> whoever do you any injury will prove, in the issue, to have done the greatest injury to themselves." (4.) It shall be an evident proof of Christ's mission: <hi type="italic">You shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me</hi> to be the protector of his church, that the promises made to the church are yea and amen in him. Christ's victory over our spiritual enemies proves that the Father sent him and was with him.
entries.8c6e5dab022749508919c688085415791e436432: <div eID="gen20787" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Zion's Prosperity Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 520.)</title> <div sID="gen20788" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion: for, lo, I come, and I will dwell in the midst of thee, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">11</hi> And many nations shall be joined to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in that day, and shall be my people: and I will dwell in the midst of thee, and thou shalt know that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts hath sent me unto thee. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall inherit Judah his portion in the holy land, and shall choose Jerusalem again. <hi type="super">13</hi> Be silent, O all flesh, before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : for he is raised up out of his holy habitation. <div eID="gen20788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20789" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Joy proclaimed to the church of God, to the <hi type="italic">daughter of Zion,</hi> that had separated herself from the <hi type="italic">daughter of Babylon.</hi> The Jews that had returned were in distress and danger, their enemies in the neighbourhood were spiteful against them, their friends that remained in Babylon were cool towards them, shy of them, and declined coming in to their assistance; and yet they are directed to <hi type="italic">sing,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">rejoice</hi> even in tribulation. Note, Those that have recovered their purity, and integrity, and spiritual liberty, though they have not yet recovered their outward prosperity, have reason to sing and rejoice, to give glory to God and take comfort to themselves. <div eID="gen20789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20790" type="x-p"/> I. God will have a people among them. If their brethren in Babylon will not come to them, those of other nations shall, and shall replenish Jerusalem and the cities of Judah: <hi type="italic">Many nations shall be joined to the Lord in that day</hi> that are now at a distance from him and strangers to him. The Jewish nation, after the captivity, multiplied very much, by the accession of proselytes to it, that were naturalized, and were entitled to all the privileges of native Israelites, and perhaps they were equal in number; and therefore Paul mentions it as an honour to him which many Jews had not, that he was of <hi type="italic">the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of the Hebrews,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.5">Phil. iii. 5</reference>. And this was an earnest of the bringing in of the Gentiles into the christian church and in that this and other similar promises were to have their full accomplishment. It was therefore strange that that should be so great an offence to the Jews, as we find it was in the apostles' times, which was promised them as a blessing in the prophets' times—that <hi type="italic">many nations</hi> should be <hi type="italic">joined to the Lord.</hi> And, as there had been one law, so should there be one gospel <hi type="italic">for the stranger and for those born in the land;</hi> whatever nation they come from, when they <hi type="italic">join themselves to the Lord, they shall be my people,</hi> as dear to God as ever Israel had been. Note, God will own those for his people who with purpose of heart join themselves to him; and, when many do so, we ought to look upon them, not with a jealous eye, but with a joyful one. Angels rejoice, and therefore so should the daughter of Zion, when many nations are joined to the Lord. <div eID="gen20790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20791" type="x-p"/> II. They shall have his presence among them: <hi type="italic">Sing and rejoice, for I come.</hi> Those to whom God comes have reason to rejoice, for he will be to them their chief joy. God will come, not to make them a visit only, but to reside with them and preside over them: <hi type="italic">I will dwell in the midst of thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.10">v. 10</reference>), and it is repeated (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.11">v. 11</reference>), because it was to have a double accomplishment, 1. In the dedication of the temple, in their regularly observing all God's institutions there and God's owning them therein. Those have God <hi type="italic">dwelling in the midst of them</hi> that have his ordinances administered in their purity, and a divine power going along with them; with these tokens of God's presence the Jewish church was blessed, after this, as much as ever. 2. In the incarnation of Christ. He that here promises to dwell among them is that <hi type="italic">Lord whom the Lord of hosts has sent</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.11">v. 11</reference>), and therefore must be the <hi type="italic">Lord Jesus,</hi> who came and dwelt in the midst of the Jewish nation, the eternal <hi type="italic">Word,</hi> that was <hi type="italic">made flesh, and dwelt among us.</hi> This was the great honour reserved for that nation in its last days; the promise of it effectually secured their continuance till it was accomplished. They could not be destroyed while that blessing was in them; and the prospect of it, according to the promise, was the great support and comfort of those who <hi type="italic">looked for redemption in Jerusalem.</hi> It is promised that when Christ comes and dwells among them <hi type="italic">they shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent him;</hi> all that were Israelites indeed were made to know it; sufficient proofs were given of it by the miracles Christ wrought, so that they might have known it, and yet there were those that perished in ignorance and unbelief, that would not know it, for, <hi type="italic">if they had known</hi> it, <hi type="italic">they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.</hi> <div eID="gen20791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20792" type="x-p"/> III. They shall have all their ancient dignities and privileges restored to them again, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.12">v. 12</reference>. 1. Canaan shall be a holy land again, not polluted by sin as it had been formerly, not profaned by the enemies as it had been of late; it shall be an enclosure again, and not laid in common. 2. Judah shall be in this holy land, shall inhabit it, and enjoy the comfort of it, and no longer be lost and scattered in Babylon. 3. Judah shall be God's portion, which he will delight in, which shall be dear to him, by which he will be served, and in which he will be glorified. <hi type="italic">The Lord's portion is his people.</hi> 4. God will <hi type="italic">inherit Judah</hi> again as <hi type="italic">his portion,</hi> will claim his interest, and recover the possession out of the hands of those that had invaded his right. He will protect his people and govern them as a man does his inheritance, and will be at home among them. 5. He will <hi type="italic">choose Jerusalem again,</hi> as he had chosen it formerly, to <hi type="italic">put his name there;</hi> he will renew and confirm the choice, and continue it a chosen place, till it must resign its honours to the Jerusalem that is from above. Though the election seemed to be set aside for a while, yet it <hi type="italic">shall obtain.</hi> <div eID="gen20792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20793" type="x-p"/> II. Here is silence proclaimed to all the world besides, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.13">v. 13</reference>. The daughter of Zion must sing, but <hi type="italic">all flesh</hi> must <hi type="italic">be silent.</hi> Observe here, 1. A very awful description of God's appearances for the relief of his people. He is <hi type="italic">raised up out of his holy habitation;</hi> as a man out of sleep (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.23">Ps. xliv. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.65">lxxviii. 65</reference>), or as a man entering with resolution upon a business that he will go through with. Heaven is his holy habitation above; thence we must expect him to appear, <reference osisRef="Isa.64.1">Isa. lxiv. 1</reference>. His temple is so in this lower world; thence from <hi type="italic">between the cherubim</hi> he will <hi type="italic">shine forth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.80.1">Ps. lxxx. 1</reference>. He is about to do something unusual, unexpected, and very surprising, and to plead his people's cause, which had long seemed neglected. 2. A seasonable caution and direction at such a time: <hi type="italic">Be silent, O all flesh! before the Lord</hi>—before Christ and his grace (let not flesh object against the methods he takes)—before God and his providence; the enemies of the church shall be silenced; all iniquity shall stop her mouth. The friends of the church also must be silent. Leave it to God to take his own way, and neither prescribe to him what he should do nor quarrel with him whatever he does. <hi type="italic">Be still, and know that he is God. Stand still, and see his salvation.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Hab.2.20">Hab. ii. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.7">Zeph. i. 7</reference>. Silently acquiesce in his holy will, and patiently wait the issue, as those who are assured that when God is <hi type="italic">raised up out of his holy habitation</hi> he will not retreat, nor sit down again, till he has accomplished his whole work.  <chapter eID="Zech.2"/> <div eID="gen20793" type="x-p"/>

entries.2b0341119b5c81e227ef3be6b513f0cde0c97688: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13031"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Zech.2.1-Zech.2.13">Zec 2:1-13</reference>. Third Vision. The man with the measuring-line.</title> <div sID="gen24463" type="x-p"/> The city shall be fully restored and enlarged (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.2-Zech.2.5">Zec 2:2-5</reference>). Recall of the exiles (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.6">Zec 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>). Jehovah will protect His people and make their foes a spoil unto them (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.8">Zec 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.9">9</reference>). The nations shall be converted to Jehovah, as the result of His dwelling manifestly amidst His people (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.10-Zech.2.13">Zec 2:10-13</reference>).<div eID="gen24463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24464" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13031"/><hi type="bold">1. man with a measuring-line--</hi>the same image to represent the same future fact as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.3">Eze 40:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.4">47:4</reference>. The "man" is Messiah (see on <reference osisRef="Zech.1.8">Zec 1:8</reference>), who, by measuring Jerusalem, is denoted as the Author of its coming restoration. Thus the Jews are encouraged in Zechariah's time to proceed with the building. Still more so shall they be hereby encouraged in the future restoration. <div eID="gen24464" type="x-p"/>
entries.9d8ce5d78df1f959ae1554c8151243933cb6a9cb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13032"/><div sID="gen24465" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13032"/><hi type="bold">2. To measure Jerusalem--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Rev.11.1">Re 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.15">21:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen24465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24466" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to see what is the breadth ... what is the length--</hi>rather, "what is to be the due breadth and length." <div eID="gen24466" type="x-p"/>
entries.1fb9b38ca279cbc17b45e318b999b05d13259b01: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13033"/><div sID="gen24467" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13033"/><hi type="bold">3. angel that talked with me ... another angel--</hi>The interpreting angel is met by another angel sent by the measuring Divine Angel to "run" to Zechariah (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.4">Zec 2:4</reference>). Those who perform God's will must not merely creep, nor walk, but run with alacrity.<div eID="gen24467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24468" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went forth--</hi>namely, from me (Zechariah).<div eID="gen24468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24469" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went out--</hi>from the measuring angel. <div eID="gen24469" type="x-p"/>
entries.4bf5a313ae5521af6b9c7d2fe1105060aacf075f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13034"/><div sID="gen24470" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13034"/><hi type="bold">4. this young man--</hi>So Zechariah is called as being still a youth when prophetically inspired [Grotius]. Or, he is so called in respect to his ministry or service (compare <reference osisRef="Num.11.27">Nu 11:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.1.1">Jos 1:1</reference>) [Vatablus]. Naturally the "angel that talked with" Zechariah is desired to "speak to" him the further communications to be made from the Divine Being.<div eID="gen24470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24471" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">towns without walls for the multitude ... Cattle--</hi>So many shall be its inhabitants that all could not be contained within the walls, but shall spread out in the open country around (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.19">Es 9:19</reference>); and so secure shall they be as not to need to shelter themselves and their cattle behind walls. So hereafter Judea is to be "the land of unwalled villages" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.38.11">Eze 38:11</reference>). Spiritually, now the Church has extended herself beyond the walls (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Ep 2:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.15">15</reference>) of Mosaic ordinances and has spread from cities to country villages, whose inhabitants gave their Latin name (pagani) to pagans, as being the last in parting with heathenism. <div eID="gen24471" type="x-p"/>
entries.157a41c52cda1fe138b149a633a6279d948b08d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13035"/><div sID="gen24472" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13035"/><hi type="bold">5. I ... wall of fire round--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Zech.2.4">Zec 2:4</reference>. Yet as a city needs some wall, I Jehovah will act as one of fire which none durst approach (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.8">Zec 9:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.1">Is 26:1</reference>).<div eID="gen24472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24473" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory in the midst--</hi>not only a defense from foes outside, but a glory within (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.19">Is 60:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.23">Re 21:23</reference>). The same combination of "glory and defense" is found in <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Is 4:5</reference>, alluding to the pillar of cloud and fire which defended and enlightened Israel in the desert. Compare Elisha in Dothan (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.17">2Ki 6:17</reference>). As God is to be her "glory," so she shall be His "glory" (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.3">Is 62:3</reference>). <div eID="gen24473" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f463513620fd3f8237a9655aeb4e1a8e3489c0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13036"/><div sID="gen24474" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13036"/><hi type="bold">6. flee from the land of the north--</hi>that is, from Babylon: a type of the various Gentile lands, from which the Jews are to be recalled hereafter; hence "the four winds of heaven" are specified, implying that they are to return from all quarters (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.64">De 28:64</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.16.15">Jr 16:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.21">Eze 17:21</reference>). The reason why they should flee from Babylon is: (1) because of the blessings promised to God's people in their own land; (2) because of the evils about to fall on their foe (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.7-Zech.2.9">Zec 2:7-9</reference>). Babylon was soon to fall before Darius, and its inhabitants to endure fearful calamities (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.20">Is 48:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.8">Jr 50:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.6">51:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.45">45</reference>). Many of the Jews in Zechariah's time had not yet returned to Judea. Their tardiness was owing to (1) unbelief; (2) their land had long lain waste, and was surrounded with bitter foes; (3) they regarded suspiciously the liberty of return given by Cyrus and Darius, as if these monarchs designed suddenly to crush them; (4) their long stay in Babylon had obliterated the remembrance of their own land; (5) the wealth and security there contrasted with Judea, where their temple and city were in ruins. All this betrayed foul ingratitude and disregard of God's extraordinary favor, which is infinitely to be preferred to all the wealth of the world [Calvin and Pembellus].<div eID="gen24474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24475" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for I have spread you abroad--</hi>The reasoning is: I who scattered you from your land to all quarters, can also gather you again to it. <div eID="gen24475" type="x-p"/>
entries.7bd29880849662dccd671283e28c0f307ec8dec6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13037"/><div sID="gen24476" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13037"/><hi type="bold">7. O Zion ... daughter of Babylon--</hi>Thou whose only sure dwelling is "Zion," inseparably connected with the temple, art altogether out of thy place in "dwelling with the daughter of Babylon" (that is, Babylon and her people, <reference osisRef="Ps.137.8">Psa 137:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.8">Is 1:8</reference>).<div eID="gen24476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24477" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">After the glory--</hi>After restoring the "glory" (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.5">Zec 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Is 4:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Ro 9:4</reference>) of Jehovah's presence to Jerusalem, He (God the Father) hath commissioned ME (God the Son, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.16">Is 48:16</reference>, the Divine Angel: God thus being at once the Sender and the Sent) to visit in wrath "the nations which spoiled you." Messiah's twofold office from the Father is: (1) to glorify His Church; (2) to punish its foes (<reference osisRef="2Thess.1.7-2Thess.1.10">2Th 1:7-10</reference>). Both offices manifest His glory (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.4">Pr 16:4</reference>).<div eID="gen24477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24478" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">toucheth ... the apple of his eye--</hi>namely, of Jehovah's eye (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.10">De 32:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.8">Psa 17:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.7.2">Pr 7:2</reference>). The pupil, or aperture, through which rays pass to the retina, is the tenderest part of the eye; the member which we most sedulously guard from hurt as being the dearest of our members; the one which feels most acutely the slightest injury, and the loss of which is irreparable. <div eID="gen24478" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf8cedb2a5d6f21e194407eca8f63e6d46787fb7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13038"/><div sID="gen24479" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13038"/><hi type="bold">9. shake ... hand--</hi>A mere wave of God's hand can prostrate all foes (compare <reference osisRef="Ruth.1.13">Ru 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.21">Job 31:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.15">Is 11:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.16">19:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.11">Ac 13:11</reference>).<div eID="gen24479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24480" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a spoil to their servants--</hi>to the Jews whom they had once as their slaves (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.14.2">Is 14:2</reference>). As the Jews' state between the return from Babylon and Christ's coming was checkered with much adversity, this prophecy can only have its fulfilment under Christ.<div eID="gen24480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24481" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sent me--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.48.16">Is 48:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">61:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.36">Joh 10:36</reference>). <div eID="gen24481" type="x-p"/>
entries.931ebdf8e4ec86df965d91c01839f89085b7d9d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13039"/><div sID="gen24482" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13039"/><hi type="bold">10. I will dwell in ... midst of thee--</hi>primarily at Messiah's first advent (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.7">Psa 40:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.9">Col 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>); more fully at His second advent (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.10">Is 40:10</reference>). So <reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zec 9:9</reference>, where see on <reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zec 9:9</reference> (<reference osisRef="Isa.12.6">Is 12:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.27">Eze 37:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.14">Zep 3:14</reference>). Meanwhile God dwells spiritually in His people (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.16">2Co 6:16</reference>). <div eID="gen24482" type="x-p"/>
entries.523211cc19117da1700918e594d822f8d8ff3111: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13040"/><div sID="gen24483" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13040"/><hi type="bold">11. many nations ... joined to the Lord in that day--</hi>The result of the Jews' exile in Babylon was that, at their subsequent return, through the diffusion of knowledge of their religion, many Gentiles became proselytes, worshipping in the court of the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.41">1Ki 8:41</reference>). Cyrus, Darius, Alexander, Ptolemy Philadelphus, Augustus, and Tiberius, paid respect to the temple by sending offerings [Grotius]. But all this is but a shadow of the future conversion of the Gentiles which shall result from Jehovah dwelling in Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.15">Psa 102:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.10">Php 2:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen24483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sent me unto thee--</hi>"unto thee" is here added to the same formula (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.9">Zec 2:9</reference>). Zion first shall "know (generally) that Jehovah of hosts hath sent" Messiah, by the judgments inflicted by Him on her foes. Subsequently, she shall know experimentally the particular sending of Messiah unto her. Jehovah here says, "I will dwell," and then that Jehovah of hosts sent Him; therefore Jehovah the Sender and Jehovah the Sent must be One. <div eID="gen24484" type="x-p"/>
entries.85e37cf01c0e9cf37cc2b34ae6f71d0d7acc50fc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13041"/><div sID="gen24485" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13041"/><hi type="bold">12. Judah his portion in the holy land--</hi>Lest the joining of the Gentile "nations to Jehovah" (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.11">Zec 2:11</reference>) should lead the Jews to fear that their peculiar relation to Him (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.20">De 4:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.9.29">9:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.9">32:9</reference>) as "His inheritance" should cease, this verse is added to assure them of His making them so hereafter "again."<div eID="gen24485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24486" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">choose Jerusalem again--</hi>The course of God's grace was interrupted for a time, but His covenant was not set aside (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.28">Ro 11:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.29">29</reference>); the election was once for all, and therefore shall hold good for ever. <div eID="gen24486" type="x-p"/>
entries.c2826a041198103694fb11c486de073c4ae2f04e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13042"/><div sID="gen24487" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13042"/><hi type="bold">13. Be silent, O all flesh--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hab.2.20">Ha 2:20</reference>). "Let all in silent awe and reverence await the Lord's coming interposition in behalf of His people!" The address is both to the Gentile foes, who prided themselves on their power as if irresistible, and to the unbelieving Jews, who distrusted God's promises as incredible. Three reasons why they must be silent are implied: (1) they are but "flesh," weak and ignorant; (2) He is Jehovah, all-wise and all-powerful; (3) He is already "raised up out of His place," and who can stand before Him? [Pembellus], (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.8">Psa 76:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.9">9</reference>).<div eID="gen24487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24488" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he is raised up out of his holy habitation--</hi>that is, out of heaven (<reference osisRef="Deut.26.15">De 26:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.27">2Ch 30:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.15">Is 63:15</reference>), to judge and avenge His people (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">Is 26:21</reference>); or, "out of His holy" temple, contemptible and incomplete as it looked then when Zechariah urged them to rebuild it [Calvin]. But the call to all to "be silent" is rather when God has come forth from heaven where so long He has dwelt unseen, and is about to inflict vengeance on the foe, before taking up His dwelling in Zion and the temple. However, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.1">Psa 50:1</reference>, 2 ("Out of Zion"), <reference osisRef="Ps.50.3">Psa 50:3</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="Hab.2.3">Ha 2:3</reference>), <reference osisRef="Ps.50.4">Psa 50:4</reference>, favors Calvin's view. God is now "silent" while the Gentile foe speaks arrogance against His people; but "our God shall come and no longer keep silence"; then in turn must all flesh "be silent" before Him. <chapter eID="Zech.2"/>

entries.2ad4ff2dd2f802868dc24686bf981cd033d434ba: <div eID="gen35440" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen35441" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35442" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35442" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35441" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35443" type="x-p"/> The vision with which this chapter opens, portended great increase and prosperity to Jerusalem. Accordingly Josephus tells us, (Wars 5:4: 2), that "the city, overflowing with inhabitants, extended beyond its walls," as predicted in the fourth verse, and acquired much glory during the time of the Maccabees; although these promises, and particularly the sublime image in the fifth verse, has certainly a still more pointed reference to the glory and prosperity of the Christian Church in the latter days, <reference osisRef="Zac.2.1-Zac.2.5">Zac 2:1-5</reference>. See Revelation 21, 22. In consequence of these promises, the Jews, still inhabiting Babylon and the regions round about, are called upon to hasten home, that they might not be involved in the fate of their enemies, who were destined to fall a prey to the nations which they had formerly subdued; God's great love and zeal for his people moving him to glorify them by humbling all their adversaries, <reference osisRef="Zac.2.6-Zac.2.9">Zac 2:6-9</reference>. The most gracious promises of God's presence with his Church, and her consequent increase and prosperity, set forth in the remaining verses, <reference osisRef="Zac.2.10-Zac.2.13">Zac 2:10-13</reference>, were to a certain extent fulfilled in the great number of proselytes made to Judaism after the return from the captivity; but shall be more fully accomplished after the restoration of the Jews to the favor of God under the Gospel. "For if the casting away of the natural Israel be the reconciling of the world, what shall the receiving of them be but life from the dead?" <div eID="gen35443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35444" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen35444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35445" type="x-p"/> A man with a measuring-line in his hand - Probably a representation of Nehemiah, who got a commission from Artaxerxes Longimanus to build up the walls of Jerusalem; for hitherto it had remained without being enclosed.
entries.023c3ce1a38655bdffcf61e6d0fbba8bb4a6f7d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen35445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35446" type="x-p"/> Run, speak to this young man - Nehemiah must have been a young man when he was sakee, or cup-bearer, to Artaxerxes. <div eID="gen35446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35447" type="x-p"/> As towns without walls - It shall be so numerously inhabited as not to be contained within its ancient limits. Josephus, speaking of this time, says, Wars 5:4:2, "The city, overflowing with inhabitants, by degrees extended itself beyond its walls."
entries.fcba7db0bc0bae143585118c3c1ba411849a9687: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen35447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35448" type="x-p"/> I - will be unto her a wall of fire - Her safety shall consist in my defense. I shall be as fire round about her. No adversary shall be permitted to touch her. Much of this must refer to the New Jerusalem.
entries.27be1f84c8960dcb7506eb3a44c73141633b2bb5: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen35448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35449" type="x-p"/> Flee from the land of the north - From Chaldee, Persia, and Babylon, where several of the Jews still remained. See <reference osisRef="Zac.2.7">Zac 2:7</reference>.
entries.4f593e481fceb9468431a21a89c26070b1f9465d: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen35449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35450" type="x-p"/> After the glory - After your glorious deliverance from the different places of your dispersion; He hath sent me unto the nations which spoiled you, that they may fall under grievous calamities, and be punished in their turn. On Babylon a great calamity fell, when besieged and taken by the Persians. <div eID="gen35450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35451" type="x-p"/> The following note I received from a sensible and pious correspondent: - <reference osisRef="Zac.2.5">Zac 2:5</reference>. "For I, saith the Lord, will be unto her a wall of fire round about, and will be the glory in the midst of her. <reference osisRef="Zac.2.8">Zac 2:8</reference>. "For thus saith the Lord of hosts, who hath sent me, the future glory (or the glory which is to come) unto the nations which spoiled you; for he that toucheth you toucheth the apple of his eye. Behold, I will shake mine hand upon them, and they shall be a spoil to their servants; and ye shall know that the Lord of hosts hath sent me. Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion; for lo, I come, and I will dwell in the midst of thee, saith the Lord. And many nations shall be joined to the Lord in that day, and shall be my people; and I will dwell in the midst of thee, and thou shalt know that the Lord of hosts hath sent me unto thee. And the Lord shall inherit Judah his portion in the holy land, and shall choose Jerusalem again. "If in the eighth verse אחר כבוד may be rendered the future, or the glory that is to come, it will harmonize with the context as a prophecy of the Messiah, whereas in our English translation the words after the glory are unintelligible. And so the Seventy. "It is evident the person speaking is distinguished from the Lord of hosts, as being sent by him; yet this person sent is also called Jehovah; and the nations who shall be joined to Jehovah in that day are called his people; and he (the person sent) will dwell in the midst of thee, (i.e., Zion), and shall inherit Judah his portion, etc. "In confirmation of my view of the eighth verse, I think Exodus 33 may be compared with it. Moses besought God that he would show him his glory; upon which it was said to him, "Whilst my glory passeth by,' I will put thee in a cleft of the rock, and will cover thee with my hand whilst I pass by; and I will take away my hand, and thou shalt see my אחר achar. Now as this was a fulfillment of Moses's request, who entreated to behold the glory, it follows that this אחר was the Divine glory, which alone he was capable of seeing. "'No man hath seen God at any time, the only begotten Son, (the Lord Jesus Christ), which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.'" - M. A. B. <div eID="gen35451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35452" type="x-p"/> Toucheth the apple of his eye - בבבת עינו bebabath eyno, the babet of his eye. This is a remarkable expression. Any person, by looking into the eye of another, will see his own image perfectly expressed, though in extreme miniature, in the pupil. Does our English word babbet or baby come from this? And does not the expression mean that the eye of God is ever on his follower, and that his person is ever impressed on the eye, the notice, attention, providence, and mercy of God?
entries.7f3ff1c90e419ba9cb18879b359aa283d003d934: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen35452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35453" type="x-p"/> I will shake mine hand upon them - I will threaten first, and then stretch out my hand of judgment against them. <div eID="gen35453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35454" type="x-p"/> A spoil to their servants - To those whom they had formerly subjected to their sway. As the Babylonians to the Medes and Persians; and so of the rest in the subversion of empires.
entries.bbe5687f2e15ed2b250e7a6db80534a6b2fb1282: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen35454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35455" type="x-p"/> I will dwell in the midst of thee, saith the Lord - This must chiefly refer to the Christian church, in which God ever dwells by the power of his Spirit, as he had done by the symbol of his presence in the first Jewish temple.
entries.7ee3c6135ac5c6919a6e76c47ddce0418712b856: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen35455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35456" type="x-p"/> Many nations shall be joined to the Lord - This most certainly belongs to the Christian church. No nation or people ever became converts to the Jewish religion, but whole nations have embraced the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ.
entries.9386dfeee4ec29334f1a7cd2c22468483a328650: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen35456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35457" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall inherit Judah his portion in the holy land - This is a promise of the final restoration of the Jews, and that they should be God's portion in their own land.
entries.21c9dfe2f6833c731b15a9ea5c4407448b7b2590: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen35457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35458" type="x-p"/> Be silent, O all flesh - Let all the nations of the world be astonished at this. God will arise, and deliver this ancient people, and bring them into the glorious liberty of the sons of God.  <chapter eID="Zech.2"/> <div eID="gen35458" type="x-p"/>

entries.e55df6ee761199a77832164567caaa1c51fbb89b: Zec 2:1-5 <div eID="gen16798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16799" type="x-p"/> Whilst the second vision sets forth the destruction of the powers that were hostile to Israel, the third (Zec 2:1-5) with the prophetic explanation (Zec 2:6-13) shows the development of the people and kingdom of God till the time of its final glory. The vision itself appears very simple, only a few of the principal features being indicated; but in this very brevity it presents many difficulties so far as the exposition is concerned. It is as follows: Zec 2:1. <hi type="italic">“And I lifted up my eyes, and saw, and behold a man, and in his hand a measuring line.</hi> Zec 2:2. <hi type="italic">Then I said, Whither goest thou? And he said to me, To measure Jerusalem, to see how great its breadth, and how great its length.</hi> Zec 2:3. <hi type="italic">And, behold, the angel that talked with me went out, and another angel went out to meet him.</hi> Zec 2:4. <hi type="italic">And he said to him, Run, speak to his young man thus: Jerusalem shall lie as an open land for the multitude of men and cattle in the midst of it.</hi> Zec 2:5. <hi type="italic">And I shall be to it, is the saying of Jehovah, a fiery wall round about; and I shall be for glory in the midst of it.”</hi> The man with the measuring line in his hand is not the interpreting angel (C. B. Mich., Ros., Maurer, etc.); for it was not his duty to place the events upon the stage, but simply to explain to the prophet the things which he saw. Moreover, this angel is clearly distinguished from the man, inasmuch as he does not go out (Zec 2:3) till after the latter has gone to measure Jerusalem (Zec 2:2). At the same time, we cannot regard the measuring man as merely “a figure in the vision,” since all the persons occurring in these visions are significant; but we agree with those who conjecture that he is the angel of Jehovah, although this conjecture cannot be distinctly proved. The task which he is preparing to perform - namely, to measure Jerusalem - leads unquestionably to the conclusion that he is something more than a figure. The measuring of the breadth and length of Jerusalem presupposes that the city is already in existence; and this expression must not be identified with the phrase, to draw the measure over Jerusalem, in Zec 1:15. Drawing the measure over a place is done for the purpose of sketching a plan for its general arrangement or the rebuilding of it. But the length and breadth of a city can only be measured when it is already in existence; and the object of the measuring is not to see how long and how broad it is to be, but what the length and breadth actually are. It is true that it by no means follows from this that the city to be measured was the Jerusalem of that time; on the contrary, the vision shows the future Jerusalem, but it exhibits it as a city in actual existence, and visible to the spiritual eye. While the man goes away to measure the city, the interpreting angel goes out: not out of the myrtle thicket, for this only occurs in the first vision; but he goes away from the presence of the prophet, where we have to think of him as his interpreter, in the direction of the man with the measuring line, to find out what he is going to do, and bring back word to the prophet. At the very same time another angel comes out to meet <hi type="italic">him</hi>, viz., the <hi type="italic">angelus interpres</hi>, not the man with the measuring line. For one person can only come to meet another when the latter is going in the direction from which the former comes. Having come to meet him, he (the second angel) says to him (the <hi type="italic">angelus interpres</hi>), “Run, say to this young man,” etc. The subject to ויּאמר can only be the second angel; for if, on grammatical grounds, the <hi type="italic">angelus interpres</hi> might be regarded as speaking to the young man, such an assumption is proved to be untenable, by the fact that it was no part of the office of the <hi type="italic">angelus interpres</hi> to give orders or commissions to another angel. On the other hand, there is nothing at all to preclude another angel from revealing a decree of God to the <hi type="italic">angelus interpres</hi> for him to communicate to the prophet; inasmuch as this does not bring the <hi type="italic">angelus interpres</hi> into action any further than his function requires, so that there is no ground for the objection that this is at variance with his standing elsewhere (Kliefoth). But the other angel could not give the instructions mentioned in Zec 1:4 to the <hi type="italic">angelus interpres</hi>, unless he were either himself a superior angel, viz., the angel of Jehovah, or had been directed to do so by the man with the measuring line, in which case this “man” would be the angel of Jehovah. Of these two possibilities we prefer the latter on two grounds: (1) because it is impossible to think of any reason why the “other angel” should not be simply called מלאך יהוה, if he really were the angel of the Lord; and (2) because, according to the analogy of <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.3">Eze 40:3</reference>, the man with the measuring line most probably was the angel of Jehovah, with whose dignity it would be quite in keeping that he should explain his purpose to the <hi type="italic">angelus interpres</hi> through the medium of another (inferior) angel. And if this be established, so far as the brevity of the account will allow, we cannot understand by the “young man” the man with the measuring line, as Hitzig, Maurer, and Kliefoth do. The only way in which such an assumption as this could be rendered tenable or in harmony with the rest, would be by supposing that the design of the message was to tell the man with the measuring line that “he might desist from his useless enterprise” (Hitzig), as Jerusalem could not be measured at all, on account of the number of its inhabitants and its vast size (Theod. Mops., Theodoret, Ewald, Umbreit, etc.); but Kliefoth has very justly replied to this, that “if a city be ever so great, inasmuch as it is a city, it can always be measured, and also have walls.” <div eID="gen16799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16800" type="x-p"/> If, then, the symbolical act of measuring, as Kliefoth also admits, expresses the question how large and how broad Jerusalem will eventually be, and if the words of Zec 2:4, Zec 2:5 contain the answer to this question, viz., Jerusalem will in the first place (Zec 2:4) contain such a multitude of men and cattle that it will dwell like <hi type="italic">perâzōth</hi>; this answer, which gives the meaning of the measuring, must be addressed not to the measuring man, but simply to the prophet, that he may announce to the people the future magnitude and glory of the city. The measuring man was able to satisfy himself of this by the measuring itself. We must therefore follow the majority of both the earlier and later expositors, and take the “young man” as being the prophet himself, who is so designated on account of his youthful age, and without any allusion whatever to “human inexperience and dim short-sightedness” (Hengstenberg), since such an allusion would be very remote from the context, and even old men of experience could not possibly know anything concerning the future glory of Jerusalem without a revelation from above. <hi type="italic">Hallâz</hi>, as in Jdg 6:20 and 2Ki 4:25, is a contraction of <hi type="italic">hallâzeh</hi>, and formed from <hi type="italic">lâzeh</hi>, there, thither, and the article <hi type="italic">hal</hi>, in the sense of the (young man) there, or that young man (cf. Ewald, §103, <hi type="italic">a</hi>, and 183, <hi type="italic">b</hi>; Ges. §34, Anm. 1). He is to make haste and bring this message, because it is good news, the realization of which will soon commence. The message contains a double and most joyful promise. (1) Jerusalem will in future dwell, i.e., to be built, as <hi type="italic">perâzōth</hi>. This word means neither “without walls,” nor <hi type="italic">loca aperta</hi>, but strictly speaking the <hi type="italic">plains</hi>, and is only used in the plural to denote the open, level ground, as contrasted with the fortified cities surrounded by walls: thus <hi type="italic">‛ārē perâzōth</hi>, cities of the plain, in <reference osisRef="Esth.9.19">Est 9:19</reference>, as distinguished from the capital Susa; and <hi type="italic">'erets perâzōth</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.11">Eze 38:11</reference>, the land where men dwell “without walls, bolts, and gates;” hence <hi type="italic">perâzı̄</hi>, inhabitant of the plain, in contrast with the inhabitants of fortified cities with high walls (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.5">Deu 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.18">1Sa 6:18</reference>). The thought is therefore the following: Jerusalem is in future to resemble an open country covered with unwalled cities and villages; it will no longer be a city closely encircled with walls; hence it will be extraordinarily enlarged, on account of the multitude of men and cattle with which it will be blessed (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.49.19-Isa.49.20">Isa 49:19-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.11">Eze 38:11</reference>). Moreover, (2) Jerusalem will then have no protecting wall surrounding it, because it will enjoy a superior protection. Jehovah will be to it a wall of fire round about, that is to say, a defence of fire which will consume every one who ventures to attack it (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Isa 4:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.24">Deu 4:24</reference>). Jehovah will also be the glory in the midst of Jerusalem, that is to say, will fill the city with His glory (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.60.19">Isa 60:19</reference>). This promise is explained in the following prophetic words which are uttered by the angel of Jehovah, as Zec 2:8, Zec 2:9, and Zec 2:11 clearly show. According to these verses, for example, the speaker is sent by Jehovah, and according to Zec 2:8 to the nations which have plundered Israel, “after glory,” i.e., to smite these nations and make them servants to the Israelites. From this shall Israel learn that Jehovah has sent him. The fact that, according to Zec 2:3, Zec 2:4, another angel speaks to the prophet, may be easily reconciled with this. For since this angel, as we have seen above, was sent by the angel of Jehovah, he speaks according to his instructions, and that in such a manner that his words pass imperceptibly into the words of the sender, just as we very frequently find the words of a prophet passing suddenly into the words of God, and carried on as such. For the purpose of escaping from this simple conclusion, Koehler has forcibly broken up this continuous address, and has separated the words of Zec 2:8, Zec 2:9, and Zec 2:11, in which the angel says that Jehovah has sent him, from the words of Jehovah proclaimed by the angel, as being interpolations, but without succeeding in explaining them either simply or naturally.
entries.60aaa76fee51bca5006ff4868de97cda6d560701: Zec 2:6-9 <div eID="gen16800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16801" type="x-p"/> The prophecy commences thus in Zec 2:6-9 : Zec 2:6. <hi type="italic">“Ho, ho, flee out of the land of the north, is the saying of Jehovah; for I spread you out as the four winds of heaven, is the saying of Jehovah.</hi> Zec 2:7. <hi type="italic">Ho, Zion, save thyself, thou that dwellest with the daughter Babel.</hi> Zec 2:8. <hi type="italic">For thus saith Jehovah of hosts, After glory hath he sent me to the nations that have plundered you; for whoever toucheth you, toucheth the apple of His eye.</hi> Zec 2:9. <hi type="italic">For, behold, I swing my hand over them, and they become a spoil to those who served them; and ye will see that Jehovah of hosts hath sent me.” </hi> The summons to flee out of Babylon, in Zec 2:6 and Zec 2:7, is addressed to the Israelites, who are all included in the one name Zion in Zec 2:7; and shows that the address which follows is not a simple continuation of the promise in Zec 2:4 and Zec 2:5, but is intended both to explain it, and to assign the reason for it. The summons contains so far a reason for it, that the Israelites are directed to flee out of Babylon, because the judgment is about to burst upon this oppressor of the people of God. The words <hi type="italic">nūsū</hi>, flee, and <hi type="italic">himmâletı̄</hi>, save thyself or escape, both point to the judgment, and in Zec 2:9 the judgment itself is clearly spoken of. the land of the north is Babylon (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.1.14">Jer 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.22">Jer 6:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.22">Jer 10:22</reference>; and for the fact itself, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.20">Isa 48:20</reference>). The reason for the exclamation “Flee” is first of all given in the clause, “for like the four winds have I spread you out,” not “dispersed you” (Vulg., C. B. Mich., Koehler). For apart from the fact that <hi type="italic">pērēs</hi> almost always means to spread out, and has the meaning to disperse at the most in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.15">Psa 68:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.21">Eze 17:21</reference>, this meaning is altogether unsuitable here. For if Israel had been scattered like the four winds, it would of necessity have been summoned to return, not only from the north, but from all quarters of the globe (Hitzig, Kliefoth). Moreover, we should then have לארבּע, <hi type="italic">into</hi> the four winds; and the method suggested by Koehler for reconciling כּארבּע with his view, viz., by assuming that “like the four winds” is equivalent to “as chaff is pounded and driven away from its place by the four winds,” according to which the winds would be mentioned in the place of the chaff, will hardly meet with approval. The explanation is rather that the perfect <hi type="italic">pērastı̄</hi> is used prophetically to denote the purpose of God, which had already been formed, even if its realization was still in the future. To spread out like the four winds is the same as to spread out just as the four winds spread out to all quarters of the globe. Because God has resolved upon spreading out His people in this manner, they are to flee out of Babel, that they may not suffer the fate of Babel. That this thought lies at the foundation of the motive assigned, is evident from the further reasons assigned for the summons in Zec 2:8 and Zec 2:9.<hi type="italic">Zion</hi> stands for the inhabitants of Zion, namely the people of God, who are for the time being still <hi type="italic">yōshebheth bath Bâbel</hi>, dwelling with the daughter Babel. As <hi type="italic">Zion</hi> does not mean the city or fortress of Jerusalem, but the inhabitants, so the “daughter Babel” is not the city of Babylon or country of Babylonia personified, but the inhabitants of Babel; and ישׁב is construed with the <hi type="italic">accusative</hi> of the person, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.22.4">Psa 22:4</reference> and 2Sa 6:2. What Jehovah states in explanation of the twofold call to flee out of Babel, does not commence with Zec 2:9 (Ewald), or with כּי הנּגע in <hi type="italic">Zec 2:8</hi> (Koehler), but with אחר כּבוד וגו. The incorrectness of the two former explanations is seen first of all in the fact that כּי only introduces a speech in the same manner as ὅτι, when it follows directly upon the introductory formula; but not, as is here assumed, when a long parenthesis is inserted between, without the introduction being resumed by לאמר. And secondly, neither of these explanations furnishes a suitable meaning. If the words of God only followed in Zec 2:9, עליהם in the first clause would be left without any noun to which to refer; and if they commenced with כּי הנּגע (for he that toucheth), the thought “he that toucheth you,” etc., would assign no reason for the call to flee and save themselves. For if Israel is defended or valued by God as a pupil of the eye, there can be no necessity for it to flee. And lastly, it is impossible to see what can be the meaning or object of the parenthesis, “After glory hath He sent me,” etc. If it treated “of the execution of the threat of punishment upon the heathen” (Koehler), it would be inserted in an unsuitable place, since the threat of punishment would not follow till afterwards. All these difficulties vanish if Jehovah’s words commence with <hi type="italic">'achar kâbhōd</hi> (after glory), in which case <hi type="italic">shelâchanı̄</hi> (He hath sent me) may be very simply explained from the fact that the address is introduced, not in a direct form, but indirectly: Jehovah says, He has sent me after glory. The sender is Jehovah, and the person sent is not the prophet, but the angel of the Lord. <hi type="italic">Achar kâbhōd</hi>: behind glory, after glory; not however “after the glory of success” (Hitzig, Ewald, etc.), still less “with a glorious commission,” but to get glory upon the heathen, i.e., to display the glory of God upon the heathen through the judgment by which their power is broken, and the heathen world is made to serve the people of God. The manner in which the next two clauses, commencing with <hi type="italic">kı̄</hi> (for), are attached, is the following: The first assigns the subjective motive; that is to say, states the reason why God has sent him to the heathen, namely, because they have plundered His people, and have thereby touched the apple of His eye. בּבת עין, the apple of the eye (lit., the gate, the opening in which the eye is placed, or more probably the pupil of the eye, <hi type="italic">pupilla</hi>, as being the object most carefully preserved), is a figure used to denote the dearest possession or good, and in this sense is applied to the nation of Israel as early as Deu 32:10. The second explanatory clause in Zec 2:9 adds the practical ground for this sending after glory. The speaker is still the angel of the Lord; and his acting is identical with the acting of God. Like Jehovah, he swings his hand over the heathen nations which plundered Israel (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.11.15">Isa 11:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.16">Isa 19:16</reference>), and they become (והיוּ expressing the consequence), i.e., so that they become, booty to the Israelites, who had previously been obliged to serve them (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.14.2">Isa 14:2</reference>). In what way the heathen would serve Israel is stated in Zec 2:11. By the execution of this judgment Israel would learn that Jehovah had sent His angel, namely to execute upon the heathen His saving purposes for Israel. This is the meaning of these words, not only here and in Zec 2:11, but also in Zec 4:9 and Zec 6:15, where this formula is repeated, not however in the sense imagined by Koehler, namely that he had spoken these words in consequence of a command from Jehovah, and not of his own accord, by which the “sending” is changed into “speaking.”
entries.3bb91769a69d5abc84d1691d9eecbdfb3f797e38: Zec 2:10-11 <div eID="gen16801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16802" type="x-p"/> The daughter Zion is to rejoice at this sending of the angel of the Lord. Zec 2:10. <hi type="italic">“Exult and rejoice, O daughter Zion: for, behold, I come, and dwell in the midst of thee, is the saying of Jehovah.</hi> Zec 2:11. <hi type="italic">And many nations will attach themselves to Jehovah in that day, and become a people to me: and I dwell in the midst of thee; and thou wilt know that Jehovah of hosts hath sent me to thee.” </hi> The daughter Zion, or the church of the Lord, delivered out of Babel, is to rejoice with joy, because her glorification is commencing now. The Lord comes to her in His angel, in whom are His name (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.21">Exo 23:21</reference>), and His face (<reference osisRef="Exod.33.14">Exo 33:14</reference>), i.e., the angel of His face (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">Isa 63:9</reference>), who reveals His nature, to dwell in the midst of her. This dwelling of Jehovah, or of His angel, in the midst of Zion, is essentially different from the dwelling of Jehovah in the Most Holy Place of His temple. It commences with the coming of the Son of God in the flesh, and is completed by His return in glory (Joh 1:14 and <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">Rev 21:3</reference>). Then will many, or powerful, nations, attach themselves to Jehovah, and become His people (cf. Zec 8:20-21; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.1">Isa 14:1</reference>). This kingdom of God, which has hitherto been restricted to Israel, will be spread out and glorified by the reception of the heathen nations which are seeking God (Mic 4:2). The repetition of the expression, “I dwell in the midst of thee,” merely serves as a stronger asseveration of this brilliant promise; and the same remark applies to the repetition of וידעתּ וגו (and thou shalt now): see at Zec 2:13. Jerusalem will thereby receive the expansion shown to the prophet in Zec 2:4; and through the dwelling of God in the midst of her, the promise in Zec 2:5 will also be fulfilled. The next verse refers to this.
entries.e1a39274922e7d358f02b157d1d0bb57ea62bace: Zec 2:12-13 <hi type="italic">“And Jehovah will take possession of Judah as His portion in the holy land, and will yet choose Jerusalem.</hi> Zec 2:13. <hi type="italic">Be still, all flesh, before Jehovah; for He has risen up out of His holy habitation.” </hi> The first hemistich of Zec 2:12 rests upon <reference osisRef="Deut.32.9">Deu 32:9</reference>, where Israel, as the chosen nation, is called the <hi type="italic">chēleq</hi> and <hi type="italic">nachălâh</hi> of Jehovah. This appointment of Israel to be the possession of Jehovah will become perfect truth and reality in the future, through the coming of the Lord. <hi type="italic">Yehūdâh</hi> is Judah as delivered, i.e., the remnant of the whole of the covenant nation. This remnant, after being gathered out of Babel, will dwell upon holy ground, or in a holy land, as the possession of the Lord.
